API providers

Grok/xAI, OpenCode Console and Go, OpenRouter, and custom API connections behind GateFox.

About 8 min read · 7 sections

On this page

API model services are upstream gateway providers. Existing clients keep their normal tool execution, permissions and instructions:

Codex / Claude / other client → GateFox → API model service

Add connection offers named presets for Grok API, OpenCode Console, OpenCode Go and OpenRouter. Each connection has its own credential and model aliases. The existing Responses, Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible choices accept other compatible services through a custom URL.

Service Gateway transport Base URL
Grok/xAI API responses-api https://api.x.ai/v1
Anthropic API anthropic-api https://api.anthropic.com/v1
OpenRouter chat-completions-api https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
OpenCode Console Responses responses-api https://opencode.ai/inference/openai/v1
OpenCode Console Chat Completions chat-completions-api https://opencode.ai/inference/openai/v1
OpenCode Console Anthropic anthropic-api https://opencode.ai/inference/anthropic/v1
OpenCode Go Responses responses-api https://opencode.ai/inference/go/openai/v1
OpenCode Go Chat Completions chat-completions-api https://opencode.ai/inference/go/openai/v1
OpenCode Go Anthropic anthropic-api https://opencode.ai/inference/go/anthropic/v1

OpenCode publishes models with different native APIs. Choose the API documented for the selected model, and create another connection when models require a different API. For example, Grok and GPT models use Responses, many open models use Chat Completions, and Claude models use Anthropic. Gemini's native Google API is outside the current three gateway transports. Model availability and routing can change; use the vendor's current catalog.

Model discovery uses the configured API's /models endpoint when available. Discovery accepts the upstream display_name or name as the model's label, including OpenRouter's published names. Internal aliases remain stable for saved chats and routing; labels do not rename the upstream model. When a published name repeats the vendor and the provider row already shows it, the duplicated vendor is dropped once: DeepSeek: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 becomes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, so the catalog row reads OpenRouter · DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. A name that does not repeat its vendor, such as Z.ai: GLM 5.3, keeps its published form. The rule is applied when discovery stores a label and when a catalog or provider list renders one, so a saved long label from an earlier release also renders without the repetition. Some services expose one mixed catalog at another URL; enter explicit model IDs when that endpoint is unavailable. The wizard supports that fallback. Never assume an entire mixed catalog works through one protocol.

For a vLLM chat provider behind a router that rejects an otherwise supported reasoning level, an operator can set "chatTemplateReasoningEffort": true on that chat-completions-api provider. The gateway then sends the caller's exact effort as chat_template_kwargs.reasoning_effort and sets enable_thinking according to the same choice. It does not map or upgrade the effort. This is opt-in because only servers whose chat template supports these fields can honor it. With the option absent, the standard reasoning_effort field is unchanged. Keep the model's advertised levels aligned with its actual template, and verify the router preserves these kwargs before enabling the option.

Grok API credits

Grok API connects with an xAI API key. API credits are managed at console.x.ai. A Grok or Grok Build browser login and its included subscription allowance are a separate authentication and billing route; the API preset does not copy that login or claim to spend its allowance.

Example provider configuration:

{
  "id": "grok",
  "label": "Grok",
  "type": "responses-api",
  "baseUrl": "https://api.x.ai/v1",
  "apiKeyEnv": "XAI_API_KEY",
  "models": { "grok/main": "grok-4.7" },
  "modelMetadata": {
    "grok/main": {
      "displayName": "Grok",
      "contextWindow": 500000,
      "inputModalities": ["text", "image"],
      "reasoningEfforts": ["low", "medium", "high", "xhigh"],
      "defaultReasoningEffort": "high"
    }
  }
}

The app stores API keys in its existing private credential files. Configuration can reference an owner-only credentialFile instead of an environment variable. Keys and request contents never go to gateway logs.

Grok's Responses API accepts function tools. The gateway converts the caller's custom and namespaced tools to stable function names on that wire, then restores the original tool identity for the caller. Custom input travels in a JSON input field; schemas, grammar guidance, forced choices and replayed tool results remain associated with their original tool. Encrypted reasoning passes through unchanged. The client continues to execute every tool.

OpenRouter Responses uses the same function-only transport on the official https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 endpoint, including DeepSeek Flash. Custom tools receive an explicit {input: string} schema instead of a native custom-tool declaration that the upstream may convert without its required input envelope. Stable, namespace-safe wire names map back to the exact caller identity; forced choices, historical calls, results and grammar guidance follow the same mapping. Arbitrary Responses endpoints and Codex subscriptions keep their native wire. Responses tool-name/catalog mismatches report the separate tool_identity_failure category. Fixed diagnostic reasons distinguish missing_tool_name, unknown_wire_tool, unexpected_tool_namespace and undeclared_tool. The error also retains the actual stream boundary and event counts. It never records tool names, namespaces, arguments or request/response content. These failures remain final: the rejected tool is not dispatched and inference is not automatically replayed. This classification does not change tool matching. Malformed custom function arguments fail before tool dispatch as invalid_tool_call, without automatic inference replay. A writer-level custom output failure also reports a provider-output error, rather than blaming the caller's request. No tool arguments or provider output are logged.

Source: OpenRouter Responses tool calling.

OpenCode conversation routing

For official OpenCode inference endpoints, all three transports identify the gateway with its own user agent and send x-opencode-session from the caller's thread ID, falling back to its session ID. The same conversation keeps that ID across tools, follow-ups and compaction. Native x-opencode-session headers on gateway ingress are also accepted as caller session IDs. A request with no conversation ID does not invent one or group unrelated requests together.

These headers are restricted to the official HTTPS OpenCode API routes; they are never added to xAI, OpenRouter or arbitrary custom origins. OpenRouter receives its own session header only at its official API endpoint, as described below. The gateway enables no provider-hosted search, shell or coding tools.

OpenRouter prompt-cache affinity

DeepSeek and Z.AI/GLM use automatic prefix caching. They do not require Anthropic-style cache markers. On the official https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 endpoint, all API transports send x-session-id from the caller's explicit session_id, then prompt_cache_key, then its existing thread/session ID. This preserves an explicit cache key's grouping, including shared fork keys. Missing or invalid identifiers do not create new identities or go into logs. The Responses transport also preserves the caller's body cache fields. For OpenRouter Responses, equivalent function/custom catalogs and namespace members use stable declaration order and schema object keys. Conversation items, tool arguments/results, schema arrays, explicit cache keys and instructions retain their values and order. Native Codex and other Responses origins keep their existing serialization.

Large cold Responses requests produce count-only api_cache_cold diagnostics. They distinguish a first measured request from changes to tool declarations, instructions, opening text or affinity. Comparisons use bounded process-memory digests; no digests, identities or request content enter logs. Stable comparisons do not prove that an upstream provider retained its cache.

OpenRouter documents this header for Chat and Responses. An explicit session activates provider stickiness on the first successful request, before a cache hit has been observed, and supplies Z.AI's session cache affinity. Without it, OpenRouter can fall back to a cache key or hashes of the opening messages. Manual provider order, endpoint eligibility and vendor cache expiry still apply; the gateway does not change provider selection or cache retention settings.

DeepSeek builds its prefix cache in the background, so a new worker's first few large requests can miss it. Set "cacheMissLimit": 6 on the OpenRouter provider to let such a worker warm up before the shared cache-safety stop.

gateway diagnostics reports cacheHit as cached input tokens divided by reported total input tokens, not the fraction of requests that hit a cache. Short/cold requests, new workers and changed prefixes can legitimately show zero. Longer cache lifetimes can charge more for writes, so the gateway leaves explicit TTL choices with the caller rather than forcing a long global TTL.

Checked 26 October 2026 against OpenRouter prompt caching, Z.AI context caching, and OpenAI prompt caching.

Self-hosted session affinity

A self-hosted Chat Completions router that hashes requests by session, such as vllm-router with consistent_hash, can keep each conversation on the worker that holds its prefix cache. Opt in with "sessionAffinity": true on that chat-completions-api provider. The gateway then sends the caller's thread ID, falling back to its session ID, as a session-id header. Subagents have their own thread IDs, so they spread across workers while each keeps its own cache.

Without this setting the router has no session key, hashes each request body, and sends every turn to an effectively random worker with a cold cache. The setting is off by default, accepted only on chat-completions-api providers, and never invents an ID for a request that has none.

Self-hosted models

Set "selfHosted": true on a loopback or tailnet provider that runs its own model. Cache safety then records repeated cache misses without stopping the worker. Leave it off for a local proxy that forwards to a metered upstream.

Context window cap

Discovery and the periodic metadata refresh copy each model's window from the server, such as vLLM's max_model_len. A self-hosted server can accept more than its clients should use, because a cold long prompt is slow to prefill. Set "contextWindowCap" in that alias's modelMetadata to keep a lower ceiling. The refresh, gateway discover --load and the Codex catalog then never advertise a contextWindow or maxContextWindow above the cap. Other discovered metadata still updates, and aliases without a cap are unchanged.

"modelMetadata": {
  "qwen/qwen3.8-flash-next": { "contextWindow": 262144, "contextWindowCap": 262144 }
}
